artifacts.name: Apollo 11 lunar module descent stage

sites.label: Tranquility Base (Apollo 11 landing site)

artifacts.status_detail: The descent stage remained at Tranquility Base after the ascent stage lifted off with the crew.

quick_facts.mass: 2,034 kg dry (descent stage); 15,103 kg for the whole lunar module at launch
quick_facts.size: Octagonal, 4.2 m across and 1.7 m tall
quick_facts.actual_lifetime: 21 hours 36 minutes on the lunar surface
quick_facts.last_contact: 27 August 1969 — the EASEP experiments it carried sent their last data

instruments.name: Early Apollo Scientific Experiments Package (EASEP)
instruments.what_it_did: A small set of experiments set up near the lander: a seismometer to record ground shaking, a dust detector, and a mirror that reflects laser pulses sent from Earth.

instruments.name: Descent engine
instruments.what_it_did: The engine burned to slow the lunar module from orbit to a gentle touchdown.

instruments.name: Landing radar
instruments.what_it_did: Measured the module's height and speed above the surface so the crew could land safely.

key_numbers.label: People who walked on the Moon

did_you_know: The descent stage stayed on the Moon. Only the upper part, the ascent stage, lifted off to carry the astronauts home.
It landed in the Sea of Tranquility, and the place is now called Tranquility Base.
artifacts.mission_context: Apollo 11 was the first mission to land people on the Moon. The descent stage did the heavy work: it carried the engine, the fuel, the landing legs and the experiments, and it was left behind when the crew departed.
artifacts.image_alt: The Apollo 11 lunar module Eagle standing on the gray surface of the Moon, with its descent stage at the bottom.

instruments.name: Passive Seismic Experiment
instruments.what_it_did: Recorded ground movements to study moonquakes and the structure of the Moon's interior.

instruments.name: Heat Flow Experiment
instruments.what_it_did: Measured how heat moves through the upper layers of the lunar surface.

instruments.name: Lunar Surface Magnetometer
instruments.what_it_did: Measured the weak magnetic field at the landing site.

instruments.name: Solar Wind Spectrometer
instruments.what_it_did: Measured the stream of charged particles from the Sun reaching the Moon's surface.

instruments.name: Suprathermal Ion Detector
instruments.what_it_did: Studied ions near the surface and how the solar wind interacts with the Moon.

instruments.name: Cold Cathode Ion Gauge
instruments.what_it_did: Measured how thin the Moon's surrounding gas is.

instruments.name: Active Seismic Experiment
instruments.what_it_did: Used small explosive charges and a thumper to probe the layers just below the surface.

instruments.name: Lunar Dust Detector
instruments.what_it_did: Tracked dust settling on equipment and how it affected the experiments.

did_you_know: It used a small nuclear generator instead of solar panels, so it could keep working through the two-week lunar night.
The Apollo 12 seismometer recorded the first artificial moonquake, made by equipment the astronauts left behind.
artifacts.mission_context: ALSEP turned each Apollo landing site into a small science station. Its instruments kept sending data long after the astronauts had gone home, giving scientists years of measurements from the Moon.
artifacts.image_alt: The Apollo 14 ALSEP central station stands on the lunar surface, with the mortar package of the active seismic experiment in the foreground and other equipment on the dusty ground around it.

did_you_know: It found the first meteorite ever identified on another planet, later named Heat Shield Rock.
It drove farther than a marathon — about 42 km — during its time on Mars.
Its mission was planned for 90 sols but lasted almost 15 years.
artifacts.mission_context: Opportunity was sent to look for signs that liquid water once existed on Mars. It kept working for almost 15 years, far beyond its planned 90 sols, and sent back evidence of ancient wet environments.
artifacts.image_alt: Opportunity rover seen from above in a self-portrait mosaic taken in 2007, with dust on its solar panels.

did_you_know: It climbed Husband Hill to study the rocks higher up.
It found rocks rich in silica, a clue that water once flowed or steamed there.
It got stuck in soft soil and could not escape, but kept doing science from the same spot.
artifacts.mission_context: Spirit landed in Gusev Crater to search for signs of past water. It climbed hills, ground into rocks and kept working for more than six years, far longer than the 90 sols it was built for.
artifacts.image_alt: Bird's-eye view of the Spirit rover's deck and solar panels on a hilltop in Gusev Crater, with the Martian landscape around it.

It was the first wheeled vehicle to drive on another planet.
artifacts.mission_context: Sojourner was a small rover carried by the Mars Pathfinder lander. It showed that a low-cost rover could drive on Mars and study rocks up close, opening the way for the larger rovers that followed.
artifacts.image_alt: The small Sojourner rover on the reddish Martian ground near a group of three small rocks, photographed by the Pathfinder lander.

It is heading toward the star Aldebaran.
artifacts.mission_context: Pioneer 10 was the first spacecraft to fly through the asteroid belt and the first to fly past Jupiter. It showed that a spacecraft could survive the trip to the outer solar system, and it kept sending signals for more than 30 years.
artifacts.image_alt: Artist's concept: Pioneer 10 flies through space with its large dish antenna and long instrument booms, with the banded edge of Jupiter in the background.

artifacts.name: Kepler Space Telescope
artifacts.status_detail: Kepler's science mission ended in 2018 after it ran out of fuel, and the spacecraft was shut down.

did_you_know: It found planets by watching stars dim, not by looking at the planets themselves.
It was NASA's first mission dedicated to finding planets around other stars.
artifacts.mission_context: Kepler was built to answer a simple question: how common are Earth-sized planets around other stars? By staring at one patch of sky for years, it showed that planets are common and found thousands of them.
artifacts.image_alt: Artist's concept: The Kepler space telescope, wrapped in gold foil with its solar panel extended, floats against a field of stars with planets and the Sun in the distance.

artifacts.mission_context: Surveyor 3 showed that a spacecraft could make a soft landing on the Moon and that the surface could support heavy equipment. Two and a half years later, Apollo 12 landed nearby and inspected it.

artifacts.mission_context: Viking 1 was the first mission to land successfully on Mars and to send pictures from the surface. Its experiments looked for signs of life and studied the Martian atmosphere and soil.

artifacts.mission_context: InSight was built to study the inside of Mars. By listening to marsquakes and measuring heat and radio signals, it helped scientists work out how rocky planets form.
artifacts.image_alt: A self-portrait of the InSight lander on Mars shows its two round solar arrays and deck instruments on reddish, dusty ground.
